distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for Acute rheumatic fever. This first-layer leaf models the acute post-group-A-streptococcal immune syndrome. Chronic rheumatic heart disease, isolated late Sydenham chorea presentations, and post-streptococcal reactive arthritis are represented only as context, late mechanisms, or mimic exposure, not as separate diagnoses inside this disease id.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Antecedent group A streptococcal pharyngeal trigger
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Recent group A Streptococcus pharyngitis or compatible untreated tonsillopharyngitis creates the immune trigger context for acute rheumatic fever.
Molecular mimicry after GAS infection generates cross-reactive humoral and cellular immune activity against cardiac, synovial, skin, subcutaneous, and neurologic tissues.
IL-6 and innate immune amplification produce fever, malaise, leukocytosis, high ESR/CRP, thrombocytosis, and anemia of inflammation.

Immune synovitis classically causes migratory large-joint arthritis, but acute rheumatic fever can also show monoarthritis, additive arthritis, small-joint involvement, axial pain, or poor NSAID response in high-risk contexts.
Inflammation of endocardium, valves, myocardium, and pericardium produces murmurs, mitral or aortic regurgitation, pericarditis or myocarditis physiology, and heart failure risk.
Rheumatic carditis can inflame the atrioventricular conduction system, most often causing PR prolongation and rarely high-grade or complete AV block with syncope and severe bradycardia.
Immune inflammation can produce erythema marginatum and painless subcutaneous nodules, usually alongside other acute rheumatic fever activity.

Cross-reactive basal-ganglia immune activity can cause chorea, emotional lability, hypotonia, and impaired motor control, often delayed after the acute GAS trigger and sometimes with little systemic inflammation.

Severe acute rheumatic fever can rarely produce pericarditis, pleuritic symptoms, pulmonary edema, pneumonitis, or alveolar hemorrhage-like imaging, usually in the setting of carditis and high inflammatory burden.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Acute rheumatic fever follows a latent immune interval after GAS pharyngitis.
Cross-reactive immune activation drives systemic inflammatory markers and fever.
Synovitis is a major tissue expression of acute rheumatic fever.
Carditis and valvulitis are central acute rheumatic fever manifestations.
AV conduction abnormalities occur during active rheumatic carditis and often improve with anti-inflammatory treatment.
Erythema marginatum and nodules are immune tissue manifestations of acute rheumatic fever.
Sydenham chorea has a longer latency and may appear after other acute inflammatory features fade.
Severe carditis and systemic inflammation can extend to pericardial or pulmonary manifestations.
A history of recent tonsillopharyngitis is an acquisition context for ARF.
Sore throat may be recalled from the preceding GAS infection or still be present if pharyngitis is ongoing.
Exudative tonsillopharyngitis can be present when GAS infection is ongoing or undertreated.
ASO or anti-DNase B elevation reflects recent streptococcal immune exposure; case JSON should keep it confirmatory unless available at the intended workup stage.
ASO titers rise after GAS exposure and support recent infection context.
Anti-DNase B titers support recent GAS exposure, especially when throat cultures are negative after latency or antibiotics.
Fever is a common minor clinical manifestation.
Historical fever is often available even when the measured temperature has normalized.
CRP rises with systemic inflammatory activity.
ESR is commonly elevated during active ARF.
Leukocytosis can accompany the acute inflammatory state or concurrent pharyngitis.
Objective inflammatory arthritis is the classic major musculoskeletal manifestation.
Joint pain may be present with or without objective swelling.
Migratory large-joint arthritis is the classic ARF arthritis pattern.
Some ARF cases show monoarthritis, additive arthritis, small-joint or axial involvement, or poor NSAID response.
Clinical or subclinical carditis is a major manifestation of ARF.
Rheumatic mitral or aortic regurgitation may be heard as a new murmur.
Mitral regurgitation is a common echocardiographic expression of rheumatic carditis.
Aortic regurgitation can occur with rheumatic carditis, often with mitral involvement.
Acute rheumatic carditis can present with pericarditis or myocarditis physiology.
Troponin can be normal in valvulitis-dominant ARF but may rise when myocarditis or myopericarditis physiology is present.
Severe carditis may impair cardiac function or cause heart failure physiology.
Valve regurgitation and carditis can lead to acute heart failure.
PR prolongation is the common ECG conduction manifestation.
Rare severe cases present with second- or third-degree AV block.
High-grade AV block can produce clinically important bradycardia.
Severe bradycardia or complete AV block can cause transient loss of consciousness or altered mental status.
Complete AV block can present with syncope or presyncope.
High-grade AV block creates acute syncope and cardiac arrest risk until inflammation improves or pacing is provided.
Erythema marginatum is an ARF major manifestation.
General rash observations should be supported when the source describes erythema marginatum or compatible plaques.
Painless nodules over extensor surfaces or bony prominences are an ARF major manifestation.
Chorea is a valid ARF manifestation but often delayed and should not redefine the acute leaf alone.
Pericarditis, myocarditis, or pulmonary involvement can cause chest pain.
Pulmonary or heart failure involvement can produce dyspnea.
Acute heart failure from severe carditis is a major short-term mortality pathway.
Untreated complete AV block can cause syncope, instability, or cardiac arrest.
Persistent valve damage is a long-term sequela of rheumatic carditis, but chronic RHD is not the first-layer acute leaf.

axes.shape_free_text: History or current evidence of recent group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis or compatible untreated pharyngitis in the ARF latency window.
Current or recently recalled sore throat.
Tonsillar exudate or pharyngeal inflammation when the streptococcal trigger is still clinically visible.
Elevated or rising anti-streptococcal antibody response such as ASO or anti-DNase B. Use as ranking evidence only in a post-workup mode or when explicitly available at the case snapshot.
Antistreptolysin O antibody titer.
Anti-DNase B antibody titer.
Measured fever during acute inflammatory activity.
Reported fever when measured temperature is absent or already normalized.
Heart rate may rise with fever or fall with high-grade AV block.
Objective inflammatory arthritis, commonly migratory large-joint arthritis but variable by risk setting.
Joint pain or tenderness during acute rheumatic fever.
Visible or palpable joint swelling from synovitis or effusion.
Migratory pattern affecting multiple joints, especially knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, or shoulders.
Non-classic ARF articular pattern such as monoarthritis, additive or symmetric arthritis, small-joint involvement, axial pain, prolonged symptoms, or poor response to salicylates.
Inflammatory synovial fluid leukocyte count when arthrocentesis is performed.
Cutaneous inflammatory eruption, including erythema marginatum when described.
Evanescent annular or marginated erythematous rash compatible with erythema marginatum.
Painless firm mobile nodules over extensor surfaces, forearms, scalp, spine, or bony prominences during ARF.
Largest reported rheumatic subcutaneous nodule diameter.
Clinical or echocardiographic rheumatic carditis/valvulitis activity.
New or compatible cardiac murmur from mitral or aortic regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation severity from rheumatic carditis.
Aortic regurgitation severity from rheumatic carditis.
Pericarditis, myocarditis, ST-elevation, troponin leak, or chest-pain dominant rheumatic carditis phenotype.
Troponin level, usually normal or mildly elevated in valvulitis-dominant ARF but potentially elevated in myopericarditis presentations.
PR interval duration on ECG.
Degree of AV block: 0 none, 1 first-degree, 2 second-degree, 3 complete heart block.
Clinically important bradycardia from high-grade AV block.
Transient altered consciousness from syncope, severe bradycardia, or hemodynamic cardiac involvement.
Syncope or presyncope from high-grade AV block or hemodynamic cardiac involvement.
Left ventricular ejection fraction, preserved in many ARF cases but reduced in severe myocarditis or carditis.
Imaging or clinical myocardial dysfunction during severe carditis.
Sydenham chorea activity. Often delayed and sometimes isolated; use timing/context to avoid distorting the acute ARF leaf.
Chest pain from pericarditis, myocarditis, carditis, or pulmonary/serosal involvement.
Dyspnea from carditis, heart failure, pericarditis, or rare pulmonary involvement.
C-reactive protein elevation during acute systemic inflammation.
ESR elevation during acute systemic inflammation.
Leukocyte count during ARF or concurrent pharyngitis.
Neutrophil count during acute inflammation or pharyngitis.
Hemoglobin may be normal or reduced by inflammation in prolonged/severe cases.
Platelet count may be normal or rise reactively with inflammation.
Hazard of acute heart failure from severe carditis and valve regurgitation.
Hazard of clinically important high-grade AV block causing syncope, instability, or cardiac arrest.
Long-term hazard that acute carditis leaves chronic rheumatic valve damage. This is a sequela path, not a separate chronic RHD disease manifold.
Lifespan hazard during acute rheumatic fever, mainly driven by severe carditis, acute heart failure, high-grade AV block, and rare severe pulmonary/serosal involvement.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: CRP and ESR share systemic inflammatory drivers but have different kinetics.
Severe synovitis often tracks systemic inflammatory burden, while the main causal driver remains upstream immune activity.
Moderate to severe mitral regurgitation increases acute heart failure risk.
Aortic regurgitation contributes to acute volume-load risk when active and significant.
Second- or third-degree AV block creates acute instability risk.
High-grade AV block increases short-term death risk when severe bradycardia is untreated.
Acute heart failure is the main short-term lethal pathway.
Active carditis increases the risk of persistent rheumatic valve damage.

treatments.clinical_role: Eradicates residual group A Streptococcus and reduces further immune triggering.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Penicillin or an alternative eradicates active pharyngeal GAS when still present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reported penicillin or beta-lactam allergy shifts selection toward macrolide or other alternatives.

treatments.clinical_role: Prevents recurrent GAS-triggered ARF episodes and recurrent carditis-driven valve damage.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Regular prophylaxis reduces future GAS trigger probability.
Preventing recurrence reduces cumulative valve injury hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carditis and valve regurgitation increase the importance of preventing recurrence.

treatments.clinical_role: Suppresses fever, arthritis, arthralgia, and systemic inflammation when renal, bleeding, and gastrointestinal context allows.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Salicylates and NSAIDs often rapidly improve rheumatic arthritis.
Anti-inflammatory treatment reduces fever and acute-phase activity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bleeding risk constrains aspirin or NSAID exposure.

treatments.display_name: Systemic glucocorticoids for severe carditis or pulmonary involvement
treatments.clinical_role: Suppresses severe inflammatory carditis, serositis, or pulmonary inflammatory extension when severity outweighs steroid toxicity.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Steroids can reduce severe carditis inflammation in selected cases.
Pulmonary/serosal inflammatory extension can improve with anti-inflammatory therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe carditis and heart failure risk increase the role of rapid inflammation suppression.
Active infection or major infection mimic changes steroid net effect.

treatments.display_name: Temporary pacing for high-grade AV block
treatments.clinical_role: Stabilizes symptomatic high-grade or complete AV block while anti-inflammatory treatment reverses conduction inflammation.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Pacing reduces immediate syncope or cardiac arrest risk from bradycardia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Temporary pacing requires procedural capability and monitoring.

treatments.display_name: Heart failure support for rheumatic carditis
treatments.clinical_role: Diuretics, afterload reduction, oxygen, and monitoring support severe carditis while immune activity is treated.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Supportive cardiac therapy lowers immediate decompensation risk.
Diuresis and oxygenation support can improve dyspnea from carditis or heart failure.

treatments.clinical_role: Symptomatic control for disabling Sydenham chorea while ARF secondary prophylaxis prevents recurrence.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Symptomatic neurologic therapy can reduce disabling movements but does not define the acute ARF leaf.

present.clinical_rationale: ARF is most common in school-age children and adolescents.
Crowding, limited access to treatment, endemic geography, and high GAS exposure raise ARF prior.
Delayed or absent treatment of GAS pharyngitis increases ARF risk.
Prior ARF increases recurrence probability and cumulative cardiac sequelae risk.
Adult-onset first attack is uncommon but real, often presenting as diagnostic mimicry rather than classic pediatric ARF.
Sydenham chorea may appear after acute fever and inflammatory markers have waned.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Structure major/minor clinical features as axes and keep final Jones adjudication as confirmatory context unless the runtime mode explicitly consumes post-workup diagnosis evidence.
Record PR interval, AV block degree, bradycardia, syncope, and pacing context when cardiac conduction involvement is suspected.
Record mitral/aortic regurgitation, ventricular function, and heart failure context; decide case-level ranking use according to whether echo was available at the intended snapshot.

Septic arthritis, infective endocarditis, Lyme carditis, viral myocarditis, Kawasaki disease, SLE, post-streptococcal reactive arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and malignancy can share individual axes.
Longitudinal prophylaxis and cardiac follow-up reduce recurrent ARF and monitor valve sequelae, but chronic RHD should remain a separate future manifold.

quality_notes: Disease-specific medical input for this distillation is only the disease name: Acute rheumatic fever.
Treatment entries avoid hand-authored priority labels; treatment ranking is left to forward simulation and outcome scoring.
Exactly one derived_hazard axis is present: mortality_hazard_in_D-RHEUMATIC-FEVER.
Chronic rheumatic heart disease is represented only as a sequela hazard, not as this first-layer disease leaf.
Sydenham chorea is represented as a delayed mechanism/axis; chorea-only late cases should be selected cautiously and should not redefine this acute leaf.
